description: Hi! I'm a high school student and really interested in these kinds of topics. I have a basic understanding of coding and graphic design, though I'm not an expert. I'm looking for team members who are ready to work together as a team with skills in programming, design, gaming, and storytelling. More importantly, I value good participation and deep involvement in the project.
summary: We developed a game where the player has to manage a Martian outpost and, with the help of a robotic dog named Laika, explore Mars remotely. The player will have to send and control Laika, whose mission is to collect information about the planet by taking pictures. It addresses the challenge by simulating real obstacles that can be encountered on such an expedition, such as choosing the right food to eat in space, proper cleaning, and where to sleep, as well as handling Mars characteristics like its terrain, dust storms, overheating, and extreme nighttime temperatures. Here, players will have to make decisions that will determine their own survival and the success of the mission. This is an important project because it helps kids apply complex concepts, understand the impact of their decisions, and learn how robotics can keep astronauts safe during space missions. Since all of this takes place inside an interactive game, it keeps them engaged throughout their learning process.
details:
Our team created Mission Laika: Across the Red Horizon, a browser game that helps students ages 7–12 understand how astronauts and engineers make decisions with limited resources. Players guide Laika, a robotic dog, through four stages of a Mars mission. They practice food safety and ventilation on a space station, choose a power source and radiation shielding before landing, collect six observation records on Mars, and explore a lava tunnel while saving enough battery to return.

We designed the levels so that early choices affect what players can do later. Choosing solar power saves energy during setup, but the rover uses more battery during a dust storm. In the lava tunnel, the flashlight helps players find objectives while drawing from the same battery they need to reach the exit. A simulated communication delay shows why Mission Control cannot respond instantly. Players can replay the mission with a different strategy and compare the outcome.

NASA’s DONKI space-weather records inform a simplified risk setting, and the game uses clearly labeled archived examples when live data is unavailable. NASA’s image archive provides Mars imagery. Curiosity’s Radiation Assessment Detector and the Mars Relay Network inform the shielding and communication activities.

The code was writed useding HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the browser edition, Canvas to render the surface and tunnel levels, Web Audio for sound effects, and localStorage to save progress on the player’s device. An earlier desktop edition uses Python and Pygame. The browser game opens without an account, an installation, or specialized hardware.

Our team considered reading level, accessibility, and classroom use. Basic mode gives students time to explore and read the feedback, while Advanced mode adds deadlines. The game supports keyboard and touch controls, larger text, high contrast, reduced motion, and sound settings. Our goal is for students to finish the mission able to explain one engineering trade-off and describe what they would do differently on their next run.
